paragraphs.source_en: At this moment, my master opened wide those dim, primeval eyes of his that I described to you yesterday, and glared fiercely at the cupboard opposite. The cupboard was six feet high, divided into upper and lower sections, each fitted with two sliding doors. The lower cupboard came right up against the foot of the bedding, so as soon as my master sat up and opened his eyes, his gaze naturally fell upon it. Looking more closely, he saw that the patterned paper on the sliding doors was torn in several places, exposing all kinds of backing paper along the pasted edges, just like entrails showing through a split belly. These entrails were of various sorts: some printed, some handwritten, some pasted backside out, and some upside down. The moment my master saw these entrails, he wanted to know what was written on them. A moment before, my master had been so angry that he wanted to catch the rickshawman’s wife and rub her nose against the pine tree; now, all at once, he wanted to read these scraps of old paper. The change seems strange, but with a hot-tempered man of this sunny, outward sort, such things are common enough and hardly surprising. It is just like giving a cake to a child who is crying and seeing him burst at once into smiles. Long ago, when my master was lodging at a certain temple, five or six nuns lived in the next room, separated from him only by a paper sliding screen. Now nuns, by nature, are the most spiteful of spiteful women; and these nuns seem to have seen through my master’s character, for they would beat time on their cooking pot and sing, in a singsong voice, The crow that was crying just now, ah, is laughing already. My master says that it was from that time on that he came to detest nuns. Whether nuns are detestable or not, the fact is that they had touched the sore spot of his fickle temper. My master cries, laughs, grieves, and rejoices with twice the intensity of ordinary people. Yet from another angle, no feeling of his has ever managed to last for long. Put favorably, he is not attached to one thing, and his mood changes quickly. But if this trait of his is translated into plain speech, in ordinary words he is nothing more than a shallow, front-door hero of a spoiled child. Since he is a spoiled child, it is perfectly natural that, after springing up with a thump in a fighting posture, he should suddenly change his mind and set about reading the entrails on the cupboard doors. The first thing that caught his eye was Hirobumi Ito standing upside down there; looking at the date above, he found it printed September 28, Meiji 11. The man who later became Resident-General of Korea seems to have been chasing after the tail of government policy even from that period. My master very much wanted to know what this gentleman had been doing at that time. When my master forced himself to decipher the parts that were hard to read, it turned out he was serving as Minister of Finance; no wonder he looked so grand. At any rate, even pasted upside down, a Minister of Finance is still a Minister of Finance. My master looked a little to the left, and this time the Minister of Finance was pasted sideways, taking a nap.

paragraphs.source_zh: 这时，主人把我昨天向您描述过的、他那双混沌不清的太古式的眼睛睁得大大的，狠狠地盯着对面的壁橱。那壁橱高有六尺，分上下两层，每层都装有两个拉门。下层的壁橱和被子底边紧挨着，只要主人一坐起来睁眼一看，他的视线就会自然而然对准这里。主人再仔细一看，那拉门上画有花纹的纸已经破了好些地方，露出了裱纸边的各式各样的衬纸，活像肚皮破后露出内脏一般。这些“内脏”，有的是印刷物，有的是手写的，有的反贴着，有的倒贴着。主人看了这些“内脏”，立刻想看看到底上边写着什么。主人方才还在发火，恨不得抓住车夫家的老婆，把她的鼻子捺到松树上去蹭，现在他又突然想看起这些旧纸头来。这一变化似乎是不可思议，其实这种事对这位阳性的易怒者说来是屡见不鲜，何足为怪。这和你给一个正在哭闹的孩子一块蛋糕，他便会立刻破涕为笑是一样的。主人过去借住在某家寺庙里的时候，隔着一层纸隔扇，邻室里住着五六个尼姑。说来尼姑这种人，在坏心眼儿的女人当中是心眼儿最坏的，这些尼姑大概看透了主人的性格，据说她们一边敲着自炊用的锅，一边拿着腔调唱道：“刚才哭的乌鸦，嘿，现在笑了。”主人说，他讨厌尼姑便是从那时开始的。尼姑可厌也罢，反之，完全是因为触到了他喜怒无常的痛处。主人哭呀，笑呀，悲呀，喜呀，都比一般人加倍地强烈。可是从另一面说，不管哪种感情，从来都没有能够长时间地坚持下去。往好里说，他不执着于一端，心情很快就会转变。但是，如果把他这种特点翻译成白话，说得通俗点，那么他不过是个肤浅的家门口英雄式的娇惯坏的孩子。既然是个娇惯坏的孩子，那么他摆出要打架的架势，“咚”的一下子坐起来之后，突然又换了心思，开始读起壁橱拉门上的“内脏”来，也就是极自然的了。首先他看到的是在那里倒立着的伊藤博文，看上边的日期，印的是明治十一年九月廿八日。他后来担任了“韩国总监”，也是从这个时期起，他就紧跟在政府的政策屁股后面了。主人很想知道这位老兄在这段时期是干什么的。经过主人把不易看清的地方勉强进行辨认后，原来是正在当大藏卿，怪不得这么神气。不管怎样，就是把他倒贴个个儿，也还是大藏卿嘛。主人又看了一下左边，这回大藏卿横贴在那里，在睡午觉。

paragraphs.source_en: That was reasonable enough; one cannot keep him standing on his head forever. Below that, in large woodblock-printed characters, he could make out only the two words, You people. He wanted to know what was printed below, but it was not exposed. On the next line only two words could be seen: Quickly, quickly. He wanted very much to know what came after that line too, but with only those two words there was no clue to go on. If my master had been a detective from the Metropolitan Police, he would have torn it off by force even though it belonged to someone else. People called detectives have had no higher education, and in order to obtain facts they will do anything. They are troublesome people to deal with. One can only hope they will show at least a little restraint. If they will not show restraint, the best course is to make sure they never get hold of the facts. I hear that they even trap honest citizens by weaving together fabricated charges. When people hired with the taxes paid by honest citizens turn around and accuse their employers, that too may fairly be called the conduct of madmen. My master shifted his gaze again and read the middle part. Right in the center, the words Oita Prefecture were turning a somersault. Since even Hirobumi Ito was standing on his head, it was only natural for Oita Prefecture to turn a somersault. Having read this far, my master clenched both fists, stretched them out, and thrust them high toward the ceiling; this was the prelude to a yawn.
